summary: Psalm 79 is a communal lament after Jerusalem has been devastated: nations have entered God's inheritance, defiled the temple, left bodies unburied, and made the people an object of mockery. The speakers ask how long God's anger will last, plead for mercy and forgiveness, ask God to answer the nations' taunt, and end by promising enduring thanks and praise.
whyItMatters: This psalm gives voice to national catastrophe inside prayer, holding together grief over violence, confession of sin, and a request that God defend his own name. In Book III of Psalms, it belongs to the collection's darker movement around sanctuary, collapse, and unanswered questions.

context.author: Associated in the heading with Asaph; in Psalms, such headings are ancient features of the collection, but their exact force can mean authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the Psalms for public and private prayer.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to all Psalms would be misleading.
context.setting: A poem oriented toward Jerusalem, the holy temple, public shame among neighboring peoples, and a community in desperate need.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic lament in an anthology of prayers and songs; it moves through complaint, petition, confession, appeal for judgment, and a closing vow of praise.

outline.heading: The city and temple are ruined
outline.note: The nations have entered God's inheritance, defiled the holy temple, laid Jerusalem in heaps, left servants unburied, and made the community a reproach.

outline.heading: How long will anger burn?
outline.note: The speakers ask how long Yahweh's anger will last and call for wrath on nations that do not know or call on him, because they have devoured Jacob.

outline.heading: Mercy, help, and forgiveness
outline.note: The prayer turns to the community's need: do not hold ancestral iniquities against us; help, deliver, and forgive for God's name's sake.

outline.heading: Answer the nations' taunt
outline.note: The speakers ask why the nations should say, “Where is their God?” and pray for prisoners to be preserved and for reproach against God to be repaid.

outline.heading: A vow of lasting praise
outline.note: The psalm closes with the people, called sheep of God's pasture, promising thanks and praise forever.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm by Asaph. God, the nations have come into your inheritance. They have defiled your holy temple. They have laid Jerusalem in heaps.
keyVerses.why: This opening names the crisis: foreign nations have entered what belongs to God, violated the temple, and ruined Jerusalem.

keyVerses.text: How long, Yahweh? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?
keyVerses.why: The verse turns disaster into direct prayer, asking whether divine anger will continue without end.

keyVerses.text: Help us, God of our salvation, for the glory of your name. Deliver us, and forgive our sins, for your name’s sake.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the psalm's plea for rescue and forgiveness and grounds it in God's name.

keyVerses.text: So we, your people and sheep of your pasture, will give you thanks forever. We will praise you forever, to all generations.
keyVerses.why: The closing vow shows that the lament aims toward restored public praise, even though the chapter does not narrate that restoration.

themes: Mercy and forgiveness for God's name

questions.question: What has happened in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter depicts Jerusalem in ruins, the holy temple defiled, and God's servants killed and left without burial. It does not narrate the event step by step; it prays from inside the aftermath. The focus is on what the disaster means before God and before the watching nations.

questions.question: Who are “the nations” in this chapter?
questions.answer: In the psalm, “the nations” are the outside peoples who have come into God’s inheritance, defiled the temple, destroyed Jerusalem, and mocked God’s people. The chapter does not name one specific nation in its own wording. Comparisons with other biblical passages may suggest a historical setting, but the psalm itself does not establish a single identification.

questions.question: What does “inheritance” mean here?
questions.answer: “Inheritance” is the psalm's word for what belongs to God in a special way. Here it is connected with the holy temple and Jerusalem, so the complaint is not only that a city was attacked, but that God's own possession has been invaded and defiled.

questions.question: Does the psalm blame only the attackers?
questions.answer: No. The psalm denounces the nations for violence and destruction, but it also asks God not to hold past iniquities against the community and asks for forgiveness of sins. The prayer holds enemy violence and the community's need for mercy together without explaining the disaster in a simple formula.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask, “How long, Yahweh?”
questions.answer: The question asks whether God's anger will continue forever. It is not calm explanation; it is a pressured lament from people who see devastation and experience God's anger as still burning. Psalms often allow this kind of direct question as part of prayer.

questions.question: Is the request for wrath and payback a command for readers to take revenge?
questions.answer: No. The speakers ask God to act; they do not describe themselves carrying out revenge. Readers differ over how to use such prayers, but the chapter itself voices outrage over bloodshed, desecration, and reproach, and places judgment in God's hands.

questions.question: Why does God's name matter so much in the prayer?
questions.answer: The psalm asks for help, deliverance, and forgiveness “for the glory of your name” and “for your name's sake.” The nations' question, “Where is their God?” makes the community's disgrace a public challenge to God's reputation. The prayer asks God to act in a way that answers that reproach.

questions.question: Who are the prisoners in verse 11?
questions.answer: The verse speaks of “the prisoner” and those “sentenced to death,” asking God to hear their sighing and preserve them. The chapter does not identify them further. Within the psalm's setting, they belong to the suffering community whose city, bodies, and worship have been violated.

questions.question: How can the psalm end with thanks after so much grief?
questions.answer: The final verse is a promise, not a report that everything has already been fixed. The people identify themselves as God's people and sheep of his pasture, then vow to give thanks and praise forever. The chapter ends in hope-filled commitment, while the earlier questions and pleas remain part of the same prayer.

glossary.def: What the psalm says the nations have entered; in this chapter it is tied to God's people, temple, and Jerusalem as belonging to God.
The sacred place the nations have defiled in verse 1; its violation is central to the psalm's grief.
Public shame or disgrace. The psalm says the people have become a reproach to neighbors and asks God to answer the reproach directed against him.
The mercy the speakers ask to meet them quickly because they are in desperate need.
The closing image for God's people, presenting them as a flock dependent on God's care.
